analysis.one_liner: Walls payday lenders off from federal consumer regulation if states license them with set fee caps.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote — it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in November 2015 and sat there until the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let payday lenders — who make short-term, high-fee loans against a borrower's next paycheck — escape regulation by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in any state that adopts a licensing law meeting the bill's minimum standards. Those standards include a 10% fee cap, a $500 loan limit, a maximum 31-day term, and a 60-day repayment grace period. The bill would also bar the CFPB from issuing or enforcing any payday lending regulation anywhere in the country for two years, and would declare compliant loans immune from being treated as unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices.
analysis.who_benefits: Payday lenders gain the most. They would get a two-year moratorium on any CFPB payday regulation nationwide, and a permanent exemption from CFPB rules in any state that enacts a law meeting the bill's requirements. Compliant loans would also be shielded from federal "unfair, deceptive, or abusive" enforcement. Borrowers in states that adopt the standards would get some new protections — a fee cap, a loan-size limit, and a repayment grace period — but only in exchange for permanently surrendering federal oversight of the industry in their state. Consumer credit counseling agencies would gain a new stream of required customers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payday lenders and credit counseling agencies

how_it_helps.text: Bars the CFPB from issuing or enforcing any payday lending regulation for 24 months after enactment, in every state [S2][S3].
Permanently exempts states with a qualifying licensing law from any CFPB regulation of payday or deferred presentment transactions, even after the moratorium ends [S2][S3].
Declares that any transaction complying with the bill and state law cannot be considered an unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice — blocking a key CFPB enforcement tool [S3].
Caps total interest and fees at 10% of the loan amount plus a $5 processing fee, limits loans to $500 and 7–31 days, and requires a 60-day no-fee grace period for borrowers who fall behind [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers. A 10% fee on a two-week loan works out to roughly a 260% annual rate, so the bill would keep a high-cost product alive while stripping away the strongest federal check on it. In states that adopt the bill's standards, borrowers would permanently lose whatever CFPB payday protections might otherwise have applied. Because a compliant transaction is exempted from unfair-and-abusive-practice law, borrowers harmed by a nominally compliant loan would have fewer remedies. The two-year moratorium would delay any federal payday rule for all borrowers, including in states that adopt nothing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Borrowers relying on high-cost short-term loans

drawbacks.text: A 10% fee on a loan of 7 to 31 days is a very high annualized cost — a two-week loan at 10% is roughly a 260% APR — so the bill's 'cap' still leaves an expensive product [S3].

The bill prohibits CFPB regulation of all payday loans for two years and permanently in states with a qualifying law, replacing open-ended federal oversight with a fixed set of state minimums [S2][S3].
Compliant loans are exempt from unfair-deceptive-abusive-practice liability, limiting the CFPB's ability to act against harmful practices that technically follow the rules [S3].
The 60-day grace period is conditional: it can end early if a borrower does not schedule and complete a course with a consumer credit counseling agency [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does include genuine borrower protections — a fee cap lower than the 15%-per-two-weeks typical in many states, a $500 loan limit, a database preventing overlapping loans, and a no-fee grace period. But the trade it offers is lopsided: those fixed minimums come bundled with a two-year federal moratorium, a permanent CFPB exemption for participating states, and immunity from the federal standard against abusive lending. A borrower paying 10% for two weeks is still paying a triple-digit annual rate, and the states' residents would give up federal oversight to get it. On balance the design protects the industry's continued operation more than it protects borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Ross introduced the bill on November 16, 2015, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S5].
Twenty-four members cosponsored it — 9 Democrats and 15 Republicans — but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed [S4][S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history after the referral, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday borrowers came out ahead of where they would have been under the bill, since the CFPB retained the authority this legislation would have suspended and narrowed. Payday lenders also came out ahead in the narrow sense that the status quo — the fee levels then allowed in most states — continued unchanged, with no new state-law route around federal rules to fight over.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Payday borrowers; CFPB authority survived intact

for.name: Rep. Dennis A. Ross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors, including five other Florida members of both parties.

for.name: 9 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, lending it bipartisan cover.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 15 Republicans and 9 Democrats, with the sponsor and five original cosponsors all from the Florida delegation — but no vote was ever taken, so no opposition positions appear in the record.

industries.note: The bill would give the industry a two-year nationwide moratorium on CFPB regulation, a permanent exemption in states adopting its standards, and immunity from unfair-and-abusive-practice liability, in exchange for a 10% fee cap that still yields roughly a 260% annual rate on a two-week loan. Its main effect is keeping the industry's high-fee business model alive and fenced off from federal oversight.
Borrowers who fall behind must schedule and complete a credit counseling course to keep their 60-day grace period, creating a mandated customer base for these agencies.
The bill requires each participating state to maintain a transaction database, which may be run by a private company, creating a new line of state-contracted business.
